entities.name: Buyid dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Buyid dynasty (934–1062 CE) was a Shia Muslim dynasty of Iranian origin (from Gilan on the Caspian coast) that seized effective control of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad in 945 CE, reducing the Sunni caliphs to ceremonial figureheads while ruling Iran and Iraq. The Buyid period is notable for its patronage of learning, Persian cultural revival, and interfaith tolerance.

When Buyid leader Muizz ad-Dawla entered Baghdad in 945 CE, he installed himself as amir al-umara (commander of commanders) while allowing the Abbasid caliph to maintain religious prestige. This arrangement — a Shia dynasty ruling in the name of a Sunni caliph — required remarkable pragmatism and demonstrated the separation of religious legitimacy from political power. The Buyids ruled three distinct regional kingdoms (Persia proper under Rukn ad-Dawla, Jibal under Imad ad-Dawla, and Iraq under Muizz ad-Dawla) in a form of shared dynastic rule.

The Buyid period saw flourishing of Persian language literature, with Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and al-Biruni doing their greatest works under Buyid patronage. Shia Twelver Islam consolidated its doctrines during the occultation of the twelfth imam, precisely during this era. The dynasty fell to the Sunni Seljuk Turks who entered Baghdad in 1055, restoring Sunni dominance.
